podcast.body: George Harrison was inspired to write this song by the gospel hit "Oh Happy Day" by the Edwin Hawkins Singers. He took great thought in writing it, anticipating that "a lot of people might get weird about it" due to fear of the words "Lord" and "God." Lyrically, the song is a risk as it pays homage to both Christianity (with "Hallelujah" in the background) and Hinduism (with "Hare Krishna" in the background), reflecting Harrison's affection for both. Musically, it was determined by a judge to have unintentionally plagiarized "He's So Fine" by The Chiffons. The song featured a prominent tambourine and went to number one in December 1970, holding the top spot for about a month. "Harrison, who's considered the third beetle, always in the shadow of John Lennon and Paul McCartney, was writing the song something? Was that just a fluke?"

podcast.body: George Harrison's 1971 song was found to sound too much like The Chiffons' 1963 song "He's So Fine." The case, which began in 1971 and concluded in 1993, determined that Harrison likely suffered from cryptomnesia, subconsciously replicating the melody. The legal battle focused on the ownership of the central melody and back royalties, making "a lot of lawyers made a lot of money from this one case that began in 1971, and like I said, did not wrap up until 1993."

podcast.body: George Harrison's song was involved in a long-running plagiarism case against The Chiffons' "He's So Fine" (1963). The judge ultimately ruled that Harrison was guilty of "subconscious plagiarism" or cryptomnesia, meaning he unconsciously replicated the melody, believing it to be an original composition, despite differences in key, arrangement, and instrumentation. The case, which started in 1971, was resolved in 1993, primarily over the ownership of the central melody and back royalties. "George Harrison got caught with this. Because it sounded way too much like this chiffon song from 1963."
